background.definition: Hand, foot, and mouth disease is a contagious enteroviral infection occurring primarily in infants and children (<10years old), characterized by fever, vesicular rash, and oral lesions.

list.listitem: Common cause of febrile illness in childcare facilities, especially in summer and fall months.
Caused by members of the enterovirus group including polioviruses, coxsackieviruses, echoviruses, and others.
Coxsackie A16 is the most common cause.
Enterovirus 71 has caused large outbreaks in Southeast Asia associated rarely with CNS disease and death.
HFMD results from direct inoculation of oral, nasal, or conjuctival tissue by oral secretions or feces of an infected person.
Viruses can be isolated from vesicular lesions, suggesting that direct viral invasion causes skin and mouth manifestations.
Fever attributed to viremia.
In the first week of illness, infected individuals are the most contagious.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Greater number of children in family

list.listitem: Hand washing can decrease transmission. A trial randomized Chinese villages to instruction in hand washing and personal hygiene vs. usual care, and found that the intervention group had a decreased incidence of HFMD (2.1% vs. 4.2%). B SORT B
A vaccine against enterovirus A71, a common cause of HFMD, has been developed in Asia but is not used in the US or Europe.
Consider HFMD in patients with a nonspecific prodrome, stomatitis, and vesicular rash involving the palms and soles. C

Differential.Differential_Features: No associated rash; oral lesions usually larger and less uniform than those in HFMD
Patients usually more ill appearing, with high fever and cervical lymphadenopathy; no rash
Also caused by enterovirus but no rash; oral lesions limited to tonsils and posterior pharynx
Oral lesions uncommon, skin lesions more centrally distributed, with sparing of palms and soles

list.listitem: Mild prodrome consisting of low-grade fever, malaise, anorexia, sore throat, and sore mouth is typical. Children may refuse to eat.

Painful oral lesions develop 1 to 2 days after prodrome, and are discrete 4- to 8-mm vesicles on erythematous base, primarily on buccal mucosa and tongue. They may coalesce to form bullae and rupture to form ulcers.

Rash appears 1 to 2 days after oral lesions: multiple 3- to 7-mm vesicles with surrounding erythema on palms, soles, dorsum of fingers and toes, and backs of hands. May also have maculopapular eruption on buttocks, elbows, knees, and/or genital area.
Assess for signs and symptoms of dehydration if patient has significant mouth pain and difficulty eating.
Patients with severe illness can present with hypersomnia, convulsions, limb shaking, and breathlessness.
Skin lesions are nonpruritic and heal without crusting or scarring.
Two-thirds of patients have oral lesions and cutaneous rash; one-third have oral lesions only.
Cold symptoms, diarrhea, and vomiting occur less commonly.
Atypical hand-foot-and-mouth disease can present with widespread vesiculobullous eruptions or erosions that are generally painless in a child who otherwise appears well.
This is generally a clinical diagnosis. Viral culture of fluid from a vesicle can identify the exact enterovirus, but clinical utility is limited since culture takes 2 to 4 weeks.
Tzanck smear is negative in HFMD and can distinguish HFMD from herpes and varicella infections.
A scoring system using 9 signs and symptoms and 11 biomarkers has been developed, but is too complex for routine clinical use.
Diagnosis is made clinically based on characteristic oral and skin lesions.

In epidemic settings, monitor for CNS involvement (irritability, headache, aseptic meningitis) and cardiopulmonary failure. These rare complications occur most commonly in the very young and in those with atypical presentations of HFMD.

Management is largely supportive with an aim to alleviate symptoms and may include over the counter medications to reduce inflammation, fever, pain. In patients with symptoms and/or signs of dehydration and unable to drink fluids, IV fluids may be necessary.
Given the contagious nature of this viral illness, children should be kept home until all of the blisters have dried.
